hb_area() Engines: INLA vs JAX on CPU and Apple GPU (Metal)

Source: vignettes/articles/hb-area-engines.Rmd
hb-area-engines.Rmd

hb_area() can be estimated by two engines:

  • inla_engine() (default): integrated nested Laplace approximation with INLA.
  • jax_engine(): full MCMC with NumPyro’s No-U-Turn sampler on JAX. It runs on the CPU, on an NVIDIA GPU (device = "cuda") or on the GPU of Apple silicon (device = "metal").

This page compares the speed of the engines and how closely their estimates agree, on one Apple silicon machine.

Setup

Item Value
Machine Darwin arm64 Apple M4
R R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24)
fastsae 1.0.0
INLA 26.8.7
JAX / jax-metal / NumPyro 0.5.0 / 0.1.1 / 0.19.0
MCMC settings jax_engine() defaults: 2 chains x 1000 draws, 500 warmup
Data sim_area_data(D = n, n_unsampled = 0, seed = 42 + n); y ~ x1 + x2
Timing Each fit run 2 times on the same data; the first run includes JAX compilation

Each engine runs in a separate R process, because JAX fixes its device at the first fit of a session. The code is in benchmarks/bench_hb_area_engines.R.

Beta (proportions) 1,000 1.7 s 104 s 149 s 149 s 1.4x slower
Beta (proportions) 5,000 3.2 s 340 s 236 s 256 s 1.4x faster
Beta (proportions) 10,000 4.8 s 659 s 314 s 328 s 2.1x faster

Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) 1,000 1.5 s 37 s 159 s 160 s 4.3x slower
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) 5,000 1.7 s 207 s 237 s 239 s 1.1x slower
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) 10,000 1.9 s 606 s 332 s 332 s 1.8x faster

The results:

  • INLA is the fastest engine at every size. It does not sample, so its time grows slowly with DD. For example, the Gaussian model at D=10,000D = 10,000 takes 1.9 s.
  • Metal has a large fixed cost per fit but grows slowly with DD. NUTS builds each trajectory in a loop whose length depends on the data, and on Metal every pass through that loop waits for the GPU and the CPU to synchronise. For the Gaussian model, going from D=100D = 100 to D=10,000D = 10,000 multiplies the Metal time by 2.7 and the CPU time by
  • CPU or GPU? The CPU is faster for small and medium numbers of domains. The GPU catches up as DD grows: for the Gaussian model Metal is faster at D=10,000D = 10,000 and above, and for the Beta model Metal is faster at D=5,000D = 5,000 and above (of the sizes tested). jax_engine(device = "auto") therefore keeps the CPU on macOS, and device = "metal" pays off only for large models.

Agreement of the estimates

The JAX fits are compared with INLA on the same data. cor is the correlation of the posterior means, max |diff| is the largest absolute difference between them, and sd ratio is the median ratio of the posterior standard deviations (JAX / INLA).

Beta (proportions) JAX CPU 100 0.99994 0.00430 1.032
Beta (proportions) JAX CPU 1,000 1.00000 0.00100 0.956
Beta (proportions) JAX CPU 5,000 1.00000 0.00054 0.961
Beta (proportions) JAX CPU 10,000 1.00000 0.00043 0.967
Beta (proportions) JAX Metal 100 0.99991 0.00340 1.032
Beta (proportions) JAX Metal 1,000 0.99999 0.00140 0.950
Beta (proportions) JAX Metal 5,000 1.00000 0.00049 0.946
Beta (proportions) JAX Metal 10,000 1.00000 0.00044 0.943
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX CPU 100 0.99999 0.02400 1.004
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX CPU 1,000 0.99999 0.01600 1.000
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX CPU 5,000 0.99999 0.02400 1.000
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX CPU 10,000 0.99999 0.01500 0.999
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX Metal 100 0.99999 0.02000 1.007
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX Metal 1,000 0.99999 0.01500 1.002
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX Metal 5,000 0.99999 0.01600 0.999
Fay-Herriot (Gaussian) JAX Metal 10,000 0.99999 0.01800 0.999

The posterior means of both MCMC engines agree with INLA, with correlations of at least 0.9999. The posterior standard deviations agree closely for the Gaussian model (ratio 1.00 to 1.01). For the Beta model they differ from INLA’s by a few percent (ratio 0.94 to 1.03, smaller from D=1,000D = 1,000 on), on the CPU and on Metal alike. This difference comes from the method and the priors, which are not identical in the two engines, and not from the device. The GPU evaluates floating-point operations in a different order from the CPU, so the Metal and CPU chains differ slightly, but they give the same estimates. The largest split R-hat over all JAX fits is 1.009.

Using the Apple GPU 

# One-time setup of the Python environment with jax-metal
fastsae::setup_numpyro_env(device = "metal")

# In a new R session: request Metal before any other JAX fit
fit <- hb_area(y ~ x1 + x2, vardir = "vardir", data = df,
               engine = jax_engine(device = "metal"))
fit$device   # "metal:METAL:0"

jax-metal does not implement two operations used by NumPyro’s NUTS sampler: the bit count popcnt, and some lax.cond statements with constant outputs. When device = "metal", fastsae replaces both with equivalent operations that Metal supports, and samples the chains sequentially. If a model still cannot be compiled on Metal, the fit falls back to the CPU with a warning.

In short: for most surveys (hundreds to a few thousand domains), inla_engine() is the fastest choice, and jax_engine(device = "cpu") is the faster way to get full MCMC. jax_engine(device = "metal") becomes worthwhile for very large numbers of domains.
